transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I, um... I hope I'm not taking up too much of your valuable time. 

I came in because... well, I don't know if I'm explaining this right, but I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It's probably just me being a bit silly, but I always feel like I have to jump up and do the next thing around the house. Even when I'm just completely worn out and I know I should just be sitting still and resting, I just have to get up. 

Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering your question okay.
When you feel this urge to jump up and do things, do you also find it hard to focus on one task, or do you often start things without finishing them?

Oh, you're... you're very insightful to ask that. I try so hard to be helpful and stay on top of things, I really do, but... well, I suppose I do get a little sidetracked sometimes. I hope that doesn't make me sound terribly lazy or irresponsible. 

Like, for instance, I volunteer with a quilting charity. If the ladies give me three or four things to take care of, I always start the first one right away—because I really want to do a good job for them! But then, I don't know, I just sort of... wander off into another little chore around the house without meaning to. And then I realize later that the last steps of what they actually asked me to do just... never got done. 

I feel so awful when I let them down like that, I promise I don't do it on purpose. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

When you find yourself jumping from one task to another, do you notice that you're doing this because you're worried or anxious about something, or does it feel more like your mind and body just won't let you stay still—almost like you can't help it?

Well, I... I suppose it's a little bit of both, maybe? I hope I'm not being confusing. I just... I like to keep busy, you know? It's good to be helpful. 

Most days, I just sort of flutter around. I'll go from pulling a few weeds in the garden, and then I'll hurry over to the senior center, and then there are always errands for the church, and then I come back and try to sort through the mail and papers at home. I just go from one thing to the next without really taking a breath. 

It's not that I'm terribly anxious, I don't think. I just... it almost feels like if I stop moving, everything will just fall apart. Or maybe it's just that my body won't quite let me sit down and rest, even when I know I probably should at my age. Does that sound like what you were asking? I really want to make sure I'm explaining it the way you need me to.

How long have you been experiencing this feeling of not being able to sit still and jumping from task to task? Did this start when you were younger, or is this something that's developed more recently in your life?

Well, I... I guess I've always been a bit of a busy bee, you know? Always on the go, always trying to make sure everyone else was taken care of. But... well, it hasn't always been this much of a bother. I hope it's okay to say that. 

It really started to become a... a bit of a problem, I suppose, a little less than two years ago. About a year and ten months ago, actually. That's... that's when my husband passed away. 

I'm sorry, I don't want to bring down the mood or make a fuss. But since then, it just feels like it's gotten so much harder to manage. The jumping around and the feeling like I can't just sit and be still... it's been causing some real trouble for me lately. I hope that's the kind of timeline you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right details.

Since your husband passed away, have you been experiencing a lot of worry or anxiety—like racing thoughts, a tight feeling in your chest, or a sense of dread—or is it more that you just feel restless and need to keep moving without necessarily feeling anxious?

Well, I wouldn't say it's exactly dread or... or anything quite so dramatic as that. I try very hard not to be a worrier, really I do. I hope I don't sound like a nervous wreck to you. 

It's just... well, honestly, it's the main reason I came in to see you. I just feel like I cannot settle down inside my own skin anymore. It's the strangest feeling. Like my body is telling me I absolutely have to jump up and do the next thing, and the next thing, even when I'm just completely worn out and know I should be sitting still and resting. 

I'm not sitting at home wringing my hands or having a tight chest, it's just this... this awful restlessness that won't let me be. I hope that makes sense? I want to be sure I'm answering your question properly.

When you're jumping from task to task, do you find yourself having specific thoughts or worries that keep pushing you to do the next thing—like thoughts that something bad will happen if you don't keep moving, or that things won't be done 'right' unless you do them yourself?

Oh, no, I... I don't think so. I hope I'm not giving you the wrong answer, but I really don't have thoughts quite like that. I don't sit there worrying that something terrible will happen if I take a break. 

And I certainly don't think I have to do everything myself just to have it done right—oh my, no, I'd hate for you to think I was fussy or demanding like that! I'm really quite happy to let others help out. 

It's just... well, my mind doesn't give me a specific reason, really. It just sort of pushes me up out of the chair to do the next chore. It's more of a... a physical urge, I guess, rather than a worry in my head. Is that helpful at all? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information.

You mentioned you've always been a bit of a busy bee, but the problem really got worse after your husband passed away. Before he died, were you able to sit down and relax without this restless urge pushing you to get up and do things, or have you always felt this way even back then?

Well, I... I suppose if I'm being completely honest, and I do want to be a good patient and give you the full picture... it's always been there, just a little bit. I hope it doesn't make me sound like a terrible student, but even way back in grade school, my teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright, but... well, a little careless. 

They'd say I was always losing my papers, or talking out of turn when I shouldn't have been. And they were always having to remind me to just stay in my seat and finish my work. I wasn't trying to be naughty, I promise! It's just... sitting still has always been a bit of a challenge for me. 

But it was manageable, you know? My husband was such a grounding presence for me. It's really only since he's been gone that this... this urge to constantly move has gotten so out of hand. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it right.

Since your husband passed away, have you noticed changes in your mood—like feeling sad, empty, or down most days—or has your mood stayed relatively the same while just the restlessness and jumping around has gotten worse?

Well, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or... or empty, exactly. I mean, of course, I miss him terribly, and it's been a very difficult adjustment, but I don't want you to think I'm just sitting around moping all day. I try very hard to keep a positive outlook, I really do. 

I haven't been feeling down in the dumps or anything like that. It's really just the... the restlessness that's been the problem. The jumping from one thing to another without finishing anything. My mood itself has been quite alright, considering everything. I hope that's the right answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need to help me.

You mentioned that sitting still has always been a bit of a challenge for you, even back in school. But I want to make sure I understand the timeline: Before your husband passed away, was this restlessness and jumping around from task to task happening at the same level that it is now, or has it really gotten noticeably worse since his death?

Well, it's definitely gotten worse recently. I mean, like I said, I've always been a little... fluttery, I suppose you could say. But it never really caused me any real trouble until my husband passed away. That was... oh, about a year and ten months ago now. 

Since then, it's just been so much harder to keep myself on track. I really hope I'm not making it sound like I'm just making excuses or letting things fall apart, because I do try my best! But yes, the... the jumping around and not being able to finish things, that's really only been causing me this much trouble since he's been gone. Is that what you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions properly.

Before your husband passed away, even though you were always a bit fluttery and had trouble sitting still, were you able to complete most of your tasks and responsibilities at home and with your volunteering—or were you also struggling to finish things back then?

Well, I... I suppose I should be completely honest with you, because I really do want to be helpful. Even back then, before he passed, I... I did struggle a little bit with finishing things. 

Like with my volunteering at the quilting charity. If someone gave me, say, three or four things to do, I'd be so eager to help! I'd start the first one right away, with all the best intentions. But then... well, I might wander off to check on another chore, or see if someone else needed a hand, and... and sometimes the last steps of what I was supposed to be doing just wouldn't get done. 

I always felt so awful about it! I really wasn't trying to shirk my duties, I promise. It's just... I'd get distracted, I guess? But my husband was always there to gently remind me to finish what I started, so it never got too out of hand. I hope that doesn't make me sound too unreliable? I really do try to be a good volunteer.

Well, I... I suppose I should be completely honest with you, because I really do want to be helpful. Even back then, before he passed, I... I did struggle a little bit with finishing things. 

Like with my volunteering at the quilting charity. If someone gave me, say, three or four things to do, I'd be so eager to help! I'd start the first one right away, with all the best intentions. But then... well, I might wander off to check on another chore, or see if someone else needed a hand, and... and sometimes the last steps of what I was supposed to be doing just wouldn't get done. 

I always felt so awful about it! I really wasn't trying to shirk my duties, I promise. It's just... I'd get distracted, I guess? But my husband was always there to gently remind me to finish what I started, so it never got too out of hand. I hope that doesn't make me sound too unreliable? I really do try to be a good volunteer.

inference.note: Ruled out F43.20 (Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and Conduct). The patient's lifelong history of inattention, distractibility, difficulty completing tasks, and restlessness dating back to childhood (teacher reports of carelessness, talking out of turn, difficulty staying seated) indicates ADHD rather than a recent adjustment disorder. While symptoms worsened after husband's death, the core pattern predates this event by decades. No significant depressed mood, anxiety symptoms, or intrusive thoughts about the loss. This is consistent with adult ADHD, likely previously compensated by her husband's structure.

opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and difficulty sustaining attention that began in childhood (teacher reports of carelessness, talking out of turn, difficulty staying seated, losing papers). While symptoms have worsened significantly following her husband's death 22 months ago, the core features predate this loss. She demonstrates persistent difficulty completing tasks, jumping between activities, and physical restlessness that is not driven by anxiety or specific worries but rather an intrinsic inability to remain still. Her husband's presence previously helped her manage symptoms. The symptom profile is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined or Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type (F90.9), with recent exacerbation related to loss of her spouse's stabilizing influence.
